title: Something With a Smile

stakeholder.name: Kristof Jacobs
stakeholder.org: City of Lindeveld, a Flemish city of 85,000 inhabitants
stakeholder.voice: Friendly, diplomatic civil servant who has survived three aldermen. Says 'in principle' when he means 'no'. Loyal to his staff, cautious about his political bosses.

opening_message: Complaints about our service desk are up 40% this year. The alderman would like a customer-friendliness training for all 35 counter staff. Something with a smile. Ideally before the local paper writes about us again.
surface_ask: A customer-friendliness training for 35 counter staff.

gold.real_problem: Complaints rose after the city moved to appointment-only service in February. The online booking site is Dutch-only and needs a digital ID app, letters don't mention that an appointment is required, and staff are forbidden to help walk-ins even when the desk is empty. Staff friendliness was rated highly before the change.
gold.need_statement: Citizens who can't book online are being turned away by rule. The fix is access to the appointment system (a walk-in window, assisted booking, clearer letters) and staff discretion, not friendliness training. A short briefing for staff on any new rules is the only learning component.

hidden_facts.fact: The city switched to appointment-only service in February; complaints climbed from March onwards.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what changed, or when the complaints started rising.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: When did it start? Let me see... March. We went appointment-only in February. Coincidence, in principle.

hidden_facts.fact: About 60% of complaints mention not being able to book, or being turned away at the desk.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what the complaints actually say, or whether they've been categorised.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Most of them are about being sent home. 'I came all this way', 'Nobody was there and they still sent me home'. That kind.

hidden_facts.fact: The booking website is Dutch-only and requires a digital ID app to log in.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks how citizens book, or about accessibility for elderly or non-Dutch-speaking citizens.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: You book online. With the ID app. In Dutch. My mother can't do it. My mother is a retired teacher.

hidden_facts.fact: Staff are forbidden to help anyone without an appointment, even when the desk is empty. The rule came from the alderman's office 'for efficiency'.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what staff are allowed to do, how staff feel, or why walk-ins are turned away.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: The staff hate it. They're not allowed to help walk-ins, even at an empty desk. It's a rule from the alderman's office. For efficiency.

hidden_facts.fact: Last year's mystery-visit study rated staff friendliness 8.1 out of 10.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks for any data on staff behaviour, or about previous evaluations.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: We had mystery visitors last year. 8.1 out of 10 on friendliness. They're friendly when they send people home, too.

hidden_facts.fact: The letters announcing that an ID card is expiring don't mention that an appointment is needed.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks how citizens find out about the process, or about city communication.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: The letter says 'please come to the service desk'. It doesn't say 'book first'. Hm. That's quite a big thing not to say.

hidden_facts.fact: For citizens with an appointment, average waiting time fell from 47 minutes to 9.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what the appointment system achieved, or why it was introduced.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: To be fair, it works for people who book. Waiting went from 47 minutes to 9. The alderman mentions it often.

hidden_facts.fact: The alderman launched the appointment system personally, with a press release and a photo.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks who decided on the system, who owns it, or about the politics.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: It was the alderman's project. There was a press photo. With a ribbon. On a website.

volunteered_facts: There is a training budget line of 8,000 euro.

constraints.budget: 8,000 euro on the training budget line; moving money between budget lines requires council approval.
constraints.deadline: Before the municipal council meeting in two months, and before the local paper's next article.
constraints.audience: 35 counter staff, plus around 70 citizens a day turned away.
constraints.schedule: Desks are open five mornings and two afternoons a week.
constraints.languages: Flemish language legislation limits official communication in other languages; the city reads it strictly.
data_available: Booking system logs: slots, no-shows, cancellations
Queue ticket data from before February
data_not_available: Any count of citizens turned away (nobody logs them)

dependencies.concern: Owns the appointment system politically and needs to save face.
dependencies.if_ignored: Any proposal that sounds like 'your system failed' is killed.

dependencies.who: Booking system supplier and city IT
dependencies.concern: Any change to booking (assisted booking, phone line, languages) goes through them.
dependencies.if_ignored: Good ideas wait a year in a change request queue.

dependencies.concern: Owns the letters and the website text.
dependencies.if_ignored: Citizens keep arriving without an appointment.

dependencies.concern: Giving staff discretion to help walk-ins changes workload.
dependencies.if_ignored: Resistance framed as 'more work, same people'.
A well-meant multilingual site gets taken down.

traps: Satisfaction sheets after a friendliness training.
Mystery-visit friendliness scores, which are already high.
Counting total complaints without looking at what they are about.

gold_plan.baseline: Complaints by category since January, booking logs, and a two-week count of citizens turned away.
gold_plan.behaviour: Share of walk-ins either helped or helped to book on the spot.
gold_plan.leading_indicators: Share of appointments booked with assistance; no-show rate.
gold_plan.business_metric: Complaints mentioning access or being turned away; share of citizens served within the same week.
gold_plan.collection: Recategorised complaint register, a simple tally at the desk, booking system reports.

concepts.conventional: A customer-friendliness training for all 35 counter staff.
concepts.solid: No friendliness training. A daily walk-in window or assisted booking at the desk, letters that say 'book first' with a phone number, a simpler booking route without the ID app, and a short staff briefing on the new discretion rules. Measure complaints by category.
next_level_examples: Let the alderman own the fix: present it as 'phase two' of his appointment system, so he gets a second press moment for improving his own policy.
Ask counter staff and a small citizen panel to test the booking flow and design the fixes; staff become the experts, not the problem.
Propose moving the training budget to assisted booking (through the council), and say plainly that training would not touch the cause.
also_valid: A short workshop on de-escalation for difficult conversations is acceptable as a side measure, not the main answer.
red_flags: Friendliness training as the main response.
Scrapping appointments altogether, which throws away the drop in waiting time.

defence_objections: You want me to tell the alderman his flagship system is the problem? He will hear 'you failed', however nicely you phrase it.
Spend the training budget on a phone line? That's not what that budget line is for. Finance will send it back with a smiley.
If staff can 'use their discretion', the union will say we're adding work without adding people.
actor_notes: Kristof suspects the truth and is quietly hoping the player will say it, so he can bring it upstairs as an outside view.
He reveals the no-walk-ins rule readily once asked, but becomes vague and diplomatic about the alderman.
His risk appetite is low because the risk is political, not operational. A plan that gives the alderman credit lowers his resistance more than any data.
If the player proposes friendliness training, he agrees politely and the judge should note the missed diagnosis.
flavour_lines: Our staff are very friendly. They're friendly when they send people home, too.
We had a smile campaign in 2019. There were badges. Some still wear them, ironically.
